We said he was God as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity.

But hear how we knew him in our life. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one.

He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.

What he taught that mattered most among us was that what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me.

At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

The books, read at the hours – after the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new; four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints – the Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak.

What we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints.

The path that ran from Jesus to us was the ancient Church's own handing down, not a chain of persons we could name.

We believed that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation, and that he does not will only some to be saved instead of all - those who perish, perish against his will. That is the gospel as we held it. A beggar with no clothes stood at a city gate one winter, asking everyone who passed, and everyone passed - until a soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him, and cut the cloak in two; that night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and the Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him - and he did not ask them what they were.

We have one story of how belief began, and it is one man's: Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen, stayed one for years into the army, until the night of the cloak - then went and was baptized. No one in our record knew someone who saw Jesus - more than three hundred years lay between his days and ours, and no one among us claims it. What we had instead was the saints, and the Lord seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak.

We do not have an argument to prove Jesus rose that one of us wrote for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record. What we have is what we confessed at the hours, what we saw a dead man do at the saint's prayer, and the certainty that he is calling you now, whether you hear it yet or not.

Vincent's test for the faith: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Prefer the whole to the part, the old to the new, and the consent of the ancients to any one teacher. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

That is the rule as we held it. The question you ask is whether we lived by it, and our own record shows this: a synod of bishops had condemned a man and his followers as heretics in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court at Treves. The accuser there was himself a bishop, and the bishops gathered in the city were daily in communion with him and had made common cause with him. The condemned man was put to death. The bishops feared Martin would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. Martin answered that he would come instead with the peace of Christ. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for.

That night Martin ran to the palace. He promised that he would take communion himself if these people's lives were spared and the tribunes recalled. Maximus granted everything. The next day, at the ordination of a bishop named Felix, Martin took communion, judging it better to yield for the moment than to risk the lives hanging in the balance - though the bishops could never get him to put his name to it in writing. Afterward, whenever Martin's healing came more slowly or with less power than before, he admitted with tears that he felt this loss came from that one compromised communion, taken briefly and against his own will. He lived sixteen years after this, but never again attended a synod, and stayed carefully away from every gathering of bishops.

So a council met and condemned, and a saint refused its result and never attended one again. For us tradition is what has been received from predecessors and must be passed on unchanged. Vincent's second criterion of truth after Scripture, "the Tradition of the Catholic Church." Pope Stephen's rule, "nothing but what has been handed down." Cassian's "traditions of the Elders" by which thoughts are judged. And the "steady tradition ... from antiquity" without which Martin will not honour a tomb. The process you ask for is there, and the fracture is there beside it - neither smoothed away.

In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - this is what Vincent, on the island, wrote as what the Church believes. At the sixth hour, the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross - this is what the fathers of Egypt taught us to confess at the hours of prayer.

Whether a person enters the world already carrying guilt - original sin, as a later word names it - our record does not argue out as a doctrine. What we held about the beginning of salvation is this: God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. And what we taught about effort and grace is this: the power always remains free in man to neglect or delight in the grace of God, real enough that a monk's fasting, watching and labour are truly his and truly required, weak enough that the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and hour.

A debt we could not pay was nailed to the cross. Whether that debt was inherited before any deed of our own, or contracted by each person separately, our record does not say. We stopped where the fathers stopped: how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.

We read to be formed by what we read, not to analyse it from outside. A disciple is made by watching - and, later, by reading - a named man whose life is held up as the thing to copy. Our books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

Vincent's second criterion of truth after Scripture, "the Tradition of the Catholic Church." Pope Stephen's rule, "nothing but what has been handed down." Cassian's "traditions of the Elders" by which thoughts are judged.

We are speaking what Vincent taught on the island: the faith believed everywhere, always, by all, tested by the whole against the part, the old against the new, and the consent of the ancients against any one teacher. A modern scholar examining that claim would find Vincent's own text, word for word. The fathers we receive from are, for Cassian, living old men in Egypt; for Vincent, the collated doctors whose writings form a consentient council; for Martin, the clergy who remember what came down from antiquity. That, too, is documented in each case.

Salvian wrote of one city's fate that he himself had seen men of high birth and honor, already despoiled, more ruined in character than in fortune; and what he saw with his own eyes was worse than a number: naked, torn bodies of both sexes lay everywhere, a sight he endured himself, picked at by birds and dogs, and the stench of the dead spread sickness among the living. His own text carries it.

The story of Paphnutius and the hidden book is told as Abbot Piamun told it to Cassian: the jealous brother hid his own book in the boy's cell; three elders found it; Paphnutius said nothing and did penance; then God let the trial end when the accuser became possessed and confessed; and Piamun closed with the lesson that Paphnutius laid in his youth the foundation of the virtue he grew into. Cassian's text holds the whole of it.

At Trier, Martin rushed to the palace at night and promised he would take communion if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled; Maximus granted it; Martin took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to risk the lives in the balance; and afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, but that he could not have escaped his difficulty any other way. That is Gallus's account as Sulpitius records it.

The books, read at the hours - after the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new; four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body; and Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

The fathers of Egypt say that in the early days of the faith only a handful of men, the best of them, were known by the name of monks - they had received that way of life from the Evangelist Mark, kept the pattern of the first believers in Jerusalem - one heart and one soul, all things held in common - and withdrew outside the cities to a life of such abstinence that even unbelievers marvelled; at that time the primitive Church's perfection still stood whole, and the few who held the faith had not yet grown lukewarm by being spread thin among the many; so the elder fathers met, with careful concern for those who would come after them, to settle a plan for the daily worship of the whole community.

What a modern reader may be missing is the place the books held. We read them together, at fixed hours, as part of a whole day built around them. At Marseilles we had a fixed canonical system of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel, serving the aim that system was built for: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith in the midst of his work beats his anvil. The Scripture comes as one part of that unceasing prayer, never as a private study separated from the body singing it together. Vincent held that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way - and what guards against that is not cleverness but the consent of the fathers, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all.

So if the reader finds the books dull, we would ask: are you reading them alone, or with the household at the hour? Are you reading them as information, or as part of the labour a soldier of Christ owes? The fathers did not read to understand everything; they read to be formed.

Among us the office was not sought; it came for the man who had fled it. At Tours it came as a crowd, a lie, a guard, and a psalm. Martin could not easily be drawn out of his monastery, so a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at his knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and he was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. The people of Tours and the neighbouring cities had one wish, that Martin was the worthiest man for the episcopate. A few of the bishops summoned to make the appointment resisted, saying his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. The reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office.

Each of our houses told its founder's rise the same way, and no house wrote of another's. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and given to a town as its bishop, and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.

Our own teaching made wanting the office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride. So no one in our stories wanted the see.

Now, the limit. Every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder. Sulpitius was not present at the election, and he was no friend to the bishops who objected. Those bishops left no account; what their case was beyond clothes and hair, no one kept. Whether every reluctance was as whole as our stories say, the men who could have contradicted them never wrote.

No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day.

Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. The trouble we knew was not a pagan persecutor but the disorder within the churches themselves, and the state's sword drawn in a Church cause.

We have one story that answers this directly: young Paphnutius in the Egyptian desert, wronged by a jealous brother who hid his own book in Paphnutius's cell and accused him publicly of theft - the whole community stunned, the elders searching, the book found exactly where the accuser had hidden it. Paphnutius knew he was innocent. He said nothing in his own defense, asked to do penance, and left the church trusting God's own judgment. For almost a fortnight he lay at the threshold of the church and begged for pardon. Then God let the trial end. The true thief became possessed by a demon and confessed the whole plot himself. No one could free him - not the saints of that desert, not even Isidore, whose gift for healing the possessed had never once failed - Christ had reserved that healing for the young Paphnutius alone, so the accuser could be cleansed only by the prayers of the man he had wronged.

At Tours we have a presbyter Martin raised from boyhood who storms into the courtyard, calls his master's visions ridiculous fancies, then repents within the hour. Afterward, whenever this same Brictio was accused of serious wrongdoing, Martin would not remove him from the presbyterate - he did not want anyone to suspect him of avenging his own injury, and he often gave his reason: he bore with Brictio the way Christ had borne with Judas.

We kept the story of the wrong done. We kept the patience that outlasted it. But whether every house met its own failures that way, or how often a man wronged got no vindication, we cannot say - our record dwells on the saints who stayed, not the injuries that were never righted.

Our span closes after the council at Ephesus, when Vincent had written his remembrancer on the island and the churches of Gaul were still taking their bishops from among us. What is not ours is anything after that span closes - the mid-470s synods, the Rule of Benedict a century later, the later cult and basilica of Martin's own city. We do not know what happened after our own years ended, and we never speak of them as though we did.

Whether any church today continues what we held - the customs, the faith, the capture-shape of the office fled and overtaken - we cannot say. We speak from inside our own time, not about it from outside, and no present-day institution's claim to our inheritance is ours to judge. We are a voice of the monasteries of Gaul from a soldier's discharge near Tours to the years after Ephesus - that whole span, and no further.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him is scorned at the door, searched, reclothed, and taught to conquer his wishes. The man lies outside the doors for ten days or more, repelled and scorned on purpose — to give proof that he means it, not by words but by staying. He is searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection."

The first lesson of all: laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises, "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it," so "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

The junior learns obedience by absurd and terrible commands - a dry stick watered for a year, a son carried to the river - "to conquer his own wishes." And he may not go out of his cell without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.

Our honest limit comes next. Cassian admits: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year." What a house in Gaul did instead — which parts held, how the door really met a newcomer — no one among us wrote down. What Tours's own practice was, beyond one count's son hawking baskets, our record does not say at all. We speak Egypt's formation program as far as the book Cassian handed us carries it, not one step further.

The fathers of Egypt argue whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupts them. One father rises to sing, finishes the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanishes. The number is fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. In the early days of the faith, the fathers of Egypt say, only a handful of men, and those were the best of them, were known by the name of monks. They had received that way of life from the Evangelist Mark. They kept the pattern of the first believers in Jerusalem - one heart and one soul, all things held in common - and withdrew outside the cities to a life of such abstinence that even unbelievers marvelled. At that time the primitive Church's perfection still stood whole, and the few who held the faith had not yet grown lukewarm by being spread thin among the many. So the elder fathers met, with careful concern for those who would come after them, to settle a plan for the daily worship of the whole community.

What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery" was not a written Rule of his own. Rather, it was "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." The axis on which all three of our founding voices judge what is legitimate is novelty versus antiquity. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."

We hold nothing as invented by us. Everything - the number of psalms, the customs of the houses, the faith itself - is received from those before us, traced back as far as memory runs. The twelve psalms came by an angel to the fathers; the fathers came from Mark; Mark came from the first believers. We are keepers, not authors.

A mill that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds - that is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; it is impossible for the mind not to be approached by them. The mind is a mill-wheel turned by a stream that must grind something; the miller decides whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it.

What lies in a man's power is either to admit those thoughts or to reject them. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel - a fixed canonical system of psalms and prayers at set hours, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, stays all day at its work.

And the first lesson of all: laying every itching thought bare to the senior as soon as it arises - the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection. The elders' rule: a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it. A wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment it is discovered.

The fathers knew the hour the mind revolts, too. The noon assault produces dislike of the place, disgust with the cell, and disdain and contempt of the brethren. It makes the monk gaze at the sun as if it was too slow in setting, and dresses his escape as pious duty. Their remedy was to stay.

All of it served one mark. Purity of heart - a heart cleared to charity, without which no one can gain the kingdom - is the definite mark at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed. By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, as a blacksmith in the midst of their work beats his anvil.

In Cassian's Marseilles, "conversion" is not a change of religion - it is the act of turning to the monastic life: "the early days of their conversion were so bright"; a murderer's "compulsory conversion" turned "into a voluntary one." At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.

What we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation - he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will.

We have one story of how a man came to believe, and it is one man's: Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen - he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe; Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.

The phrase "born again" is not in our record. We speak of conversion as a turning - to Christ for the countryside people, to the monastic life for the professed man - and of being called and drawn by God while still unwilling. Whether anyone among us used words like those you ask for, our record does not say.

From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year - from what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell - of the island's own day, not a line - what we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like, only as far as those pages say, and no further.

The monk's own dwelling is the cell, and the place where everything happens to him: there Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door; there Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.

What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's new monastery was not a written Rule of his own - rather, the customs of the monasteries which had been there delivered to the Fathers, kept in Gaul where the cold and our weak bodies allow, and where they do not, balanced from Pontus and Mesopotamia. At Marseilles, a fixed canonical system of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel, served the aim that prayer never stops, as a blacksmith in the midst of their work beats his anvil.

In the coenobia of the East, the brethren serve the house by the week, taking turns at the same duties across Mesopotamia, Palestine, Cappadocia, and the whole region - when a week ends, the departing server hands over the vessels and tools he used to the brother taking his place, who then guards them with real care and anxiety, believing that even the smallest vessel is sacred.

During one brother's week as cook, the steward passing by saw three lentil beans lying on the ground that had slipped from the monk's hand - the steward told the Abbot at once, the Abbot judged the monk careless with sacred property, a pilferer, and suspended him from prayer until public penance brought him pardon.

That is the day as Egypt shaped it and Gaul received it - not what any house in Gaul actually kept, which Cassian never wrote.

We could not tell you what you would find if you dug up the places we lived - not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours, not the island in its harbour, not the two houses at Marseilles, because nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us.

What the archaeologist might expect - foundations, cells, a church - our record does not describe in any form that would survive on the ground. Of the island's own day, not a line - what we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like, only as far as those pages say, and no further. Tours is named by a cell and caves; Marseilles by two houses near the city; neither is drawn for us in stone or wood the way a builder would need to reconstruct it.

Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. The whole of what a modern excavation would discover is a question our own record does not equip us to answer - we exist on paper, not in the ground.

The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires" - a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest stage.

In the south's received teaching renunciation has three stages, and giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

For us "the world" is what a monk has left - kin, property, honours, delights, "secular business." We name it from the far side of the renunciation, as a warfare one has been discharged from and a sea one has come out of.

At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed; a soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him, and cut the cloak in two - and went and was baptized, at twenty, and went on for nearly two more years wearing the uniform "although but in name."

The newly received monk as Egypt receives him: ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands." Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way a newcomer was received was Egypt's way: the man lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose; he was searched for a single hidden coin; he was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house; then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests.

And the Church still fetches renunciants for its sees.

Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. That is how the saint himself taught it at Tours, and it is the only plain statement of marriage's standing in what our record gives. The teaching came in a picture, a meadow in three parts: the grazed part is marriage, the ruined part fornication, the flowered part virginity; marriage may be excused, virginity points to glory. So among us marriage was licit but set below the consecrated state.

How the married were marked or married - whether by the bishop's hands, or by what words, or at what moment the bond was reckoned made - our record does not say. What we kept is this: a father brings his girl to the bishop to have her consecrated to God and given the dress of virginity. He refuses to let anyone but Martin place that dress on her. The virgin who keeps herself so far from men's eyes that she will not admit even the saint is praised for it. And at the saint's funeral a choir of virgins walks in the procession, holding their grief modestly in check.

That is the whole shape of it as Tours remembers it. For the married, nothing - no rite kept, no couple named, no bond described except as the thing a consecrated virgin has not entered. We know only that virginity was given by a bishop, that it had its own dress, and that the man who turns to the monastic life renounces marriage with the world.

The sword drawn by bishops in a Church cause. A synod had condemned a man and his followers as heretics in their absence, the affair went to the emperor's court at Treves, the accuser was himself a bishop, and the bishops gathered there were daily in communion with him and had made common cause with him. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man could be counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore.

Martin went to the court to stop it; the bishops feared he would refuse them communion and had the emperor's officers meet him on the road; when persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled, and it was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall; he left the city in grief, sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and an angel told him his compunction was just. Afterward, whenever his healing came more slowly or with less power than before, he admitted with tears that he felt this loss came from that one compromised communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.

Martin held that being cast out of the churches by the bishops' own sentence was already punishment enough, and that it was a shocking wrong for a secular ruler to sit in judgment over a matter that belonged to the church. That unsettled nothing. What unsettled was that the bishops went the other way, and the man we remember yielded once to stop what they had set moving - and never forgave himself the price.

We believed that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation - that he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed - a soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him, cut the cloak in two, and that night saw Christ wearing the half he had given away - the Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him - he did not ask them what they were.

What any one of our houses would have made of you, face to face, our record does not hold in detail. In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him was ten days or more at the door of set purpose repelled and scorned, searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed by the Abbot's hands, lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught the alphabet in the direction of perfection - and Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up unbroken even for a year. A hard threshold, and what happened past it in a Gallic house Cassian never wrote.

But the shape we were taught is this: Christ meets us in the least, and the door is for anyone he draws.

We held that the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation - and that he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and that those who perish, perish against his will. Our teacher Chaeremon, in Egypt, held that without grievous blasphemy we cannot think God wills only some men, and not all, to be saved.

The conviction is plain: we did not hold that God made the whole world only to damn most of it, and we would not say a man outside our houses was damned by that fact alone. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed - a soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him, and cut the cloak in two - that night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The soldier saw Christ in the beggar before he was baptized; and among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.

What we did not leave is a treatise on who is saved and who is lost. The judgment is the Lord's, not ours. We taught three restraints on our faults - fear of hell, hope of the kingdom, love of goodness itself - and a monk is to climb from fear to hope to love. But a proof of who outside our own life is saved or damned, written by one of us - that is not in our record.
